title: Socrates and Phaedo: Philosophy as the Triumph Over Fear of Death
summary: Drinking the lethal cup of hemlock in 399 BCE, Socrates comforted his weeping disciples, demonstrating that a life dedicated to truth transcends physical mortality.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 165: ரகசியக் கடிதம் கசிந்தபின் நேருவின் பதில்
full_text:
As the sun dipped behind the Athenian hills in 399 BCE, the final hour of Socrates arrived inside the state prison.

The jailer entered with a bronze cup containing the lethal hemlock potion. Around the philosopher stood his beloved companions—Phaedo, Crito, Apollodorus, and others—their faces wet with tears. Some wept aloud in uncontrollable grief.

Socrates took the cup steadily, his hands without a tremor, and looked at his distraught disciples with gentle reproach:
"What is this strange behavior, my dear friends? I sent the women away precisely that we might avoid such lamentation, for I have heard that a person should meet his end in peaceful silence. Be calm and show fortitude!"

Ashamed, the companions checked their weeping. Crito stepped forward and asked softly: "How shall we bury you, Socrates?"

Socrates chuckled with characteristic humor:
"Any way you wish, Crito—if only you can catch me and I do not slip through your fingers!
You speak as if this mortal corpse of flesh and bone is Socrates. As soon as the poison does its work, I shall depart for the joy of the blessed. When you lay my body in the earth, do not say that you are burying Socrates. Say only that you are burying my vessel. My ideas, my search for truth, and my spirit remain utterly beyond the reach of graves and tyrants!"

Walking across the cell until his legs grew heavy, Socrates lay down. As numbness reached his chest, he uncovered his face to whisper his famous final words to Crito:
"Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius; pay the debt and do not forget it." (A traditional Greek offering of thanksgiving after recovering from an illness—a metaphor for the soul’s liberation from mortal limitation).

Through his serene departure, Socrates proved that an unexamined life may not be worth living, but a life dedicated to truth is triumphant even in death.
